list.listitem: Suspect glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency in patients with acute non-immune hemolysis caused by drugs, oxidative stress or infection, as well as in infants with neonatal jaundice. C
Confirm diagnosis with a test of G6PD enzyme activity - a fluorescent antibody test for hemoglobin-adjusted NADPH or a PCR genotype test. C
Consider screening for G6PD deficiency before prescribing primaquine to at-risk individuals travelling to malaria prevalent areas. A
In most patients with G6PD deficiency, hemolysis will resolve spontaneously without complication if the offending drug/substance is removed.
Treatment is primarily supportive and prognosis is good. C

background.definition: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD) is an X-linked genetic enzyme defect of erythrocytes that is responsible for a non-immune hemolytic anemia of varying intensity, most often triggered by infections, certain drugs, or eating fava beans.

list.listitem: Approximately 400 million persons are affected worldwide.
Ten percent to 15% of American black males.

In a study of 988 school children from a conflict zone in Myanmar, G6PD deficiency was identified in 16.9%. Among all children, there was a high prevalence of anemia (73%), growth stinting (50%) and wasting (25%).

Based on community surveys, G6PDd allele frequency is 8.0% (interquartile range: 7.4-8.8) across malaria endemic countries. In another study of 2045 patients with malaria recruited from six African countries, G6PD deficiency prevalence was 9.0% (7.2% male hemizygous and 1.8% female homozygous); just over one quarter of the women (273/1027) were heterozygous for G6PD deficiency.
It is the most common enzyme disorder of human erythrocytes.
Sixty-six G6PD-deficient Brazilian males in a screening study had higher rates of impaired fasting glucose (39.4% vs. 6.8%) and diabetes (22.7% vs. 6.1%) compaired to 132 G6PD-normal males.
Individuals with G6PD deficiency may be at lower risk of colon cancer (odds ratio 0.57, 95% confidence interval 0.37-0.87).

Blood that is donated and stored for 42 days from patients with G6PD deficiency exhibited significantly lower 24-hour posttransfusion red blood cell (RBC) recovery compared to control volunteer blood (78.5% vs. 85.3%, respectively) and samples from 3 patients fell below the 5% FDA acceptability criterion for stored donor RBCs.
Variations in gene mutations that code for G6PD activity. As an x-linked disorder, it primarily affects men but can affect women and hemolytic attacks can occur in heterozygotes.

Thirteen different haplotypes (combination of alleles [DNA sequences] located near each other on a chromosome and inherited together) have been identified and may be useful in understanding disease severity.

In a study of 86 Ethiopian patients with malaria, a common G6PD mutation A376G was found in 20 patients, including 19 heterozygous females and 1 hemizygous male, an uncommon missense mutations was found in 2 heterozygous females, a mutation in the intronic region in 1 male, and a newly reported intronic-region mutation at chrX:154535443(C→T) in 2 heterozygous females. In a study in Fujian Province, China, of 904 neonates with abnormal G6PD enzyme activity, 17 mutation types were detected including 15 single point mutations and 7 complex mutations.
G6PD A: usually class III (see diagnostic criteria below) and found primarily in blacks.
G6PD Mediterranean: usually class II and found in persons of Mediterranean descent.
Also seen in persons of Asian ethnicity.
X-linked disorder characterized by an inability to catalyze the first step of the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt.
Reduced ability to produce nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphatase (NADPH) from NADP, and therefore poor resistance to oxidative stress on erythrocytes.
Patients with G6PD deficiency should avoid exposure to known oxidative drugs () and fava beans. A

Screening of at-risk individuals prior to administration of known oxidative drugs may be warranted. C
This is particularly important when prescribing primaquine, the only drug active against the dormant relapsing forms of Plasmodium vivax, and for treatment of infectious P. falciparum gametocytes. Hemolytic anemia can occur when using this drug even in those with normal G6PD status; in one retrospective study, a drop of hemoglobin >25% associated with severe anemia occurred in 0.3% (1/389) of patients on chloroquine plus primaquine.

Giving a single dose of primaquine may be safe for patients with G6PD deficiency. In a safety trial of 51 males, both adults and children, there were no cases of symptomatic hemolysis and 4 cases with mild adverse events. The mean largest within-person percentage change in hemoglobin level between days 0 and 10 was -9.7% (95% CI -13.5% to -5.90%) in G6PD-deficient adults receiving 0.50 mg/kg of primaquine, -11.5% (95% CI -16.1% to -6.96%) in G6PD-deficient boys aged 11-17 years, and -9.61% (95% CI -7.59% to -13.9%) in G6PD-deficient boys aged 5-10 years. In a Cambodian open-label RCT of patients with malaria, the addition of a single dose of primaquine did not affect day 7 nadir hemoglobin levels based on G6PD deficiency status (9 with G6PD deficiency vs. 46 normal G6PD); low levels were associated with initial hemoglobin level and higher parasitemia.
Suspect G6PD deficiency in cases of acute non-immune hemolysis caused by drugs, oxidative stress or infection. C
Suspect G6PD deficiency in severe neonatal jaundice in descendants of populations known to be at high risk. C
To confirm G6PD deficiency, order a test of G6PD enzyme activity - a fluorescent antibody test for hemoglobin-adjusted NADPH or a PCR genotype test.

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive Coombs test excludes G6PD deficiency
Elevated transaminases and positive hepatitis tests
Positive sickle test, more severe disease (generally)

list.listitem: G6PD mutations are divided into 5 classes by the World Health Organization (1989) based on degree of enzyme deficiency and severity of hemolytic anemia. At the October 2019 meeting of the Malaria Policy Advisory Committee in Geneva, a recommendation was made to convene a technical consultation to revise the criteria and address the question of what assessment of G6PD activity should be required prior to administration of primaquine or tafenoquine. The current classification scheme is as follows:. Class I severe enzyme deficiency (<10% residual activity) with chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia. Class II severe enzyme deficiency with intermittent hemolytic anemia. Class III moderate deficiency (10% to 60% residual activity) causing hemolysis with stressors only. Class IV non-deficient variant (60% to 150%) with no clinical manifestations. Class V increased enzyme activity.
Consider G6PD deficiency in any patient who presents with hemolytic anemia.

The typical patient presents with jaundice and mild anemia after infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, or other physiological stress. Less commonly individuals present after ingesting precipitating foods or medications, or after strenuous excercise.
On physical examination, jaundice or splenomegaly may be seen but the frequency of specific symptoms is not available in the literature.
Neonates can present with hyperbilirubinemia in the first 4 days of life.

Most patients present with hemolytic anemia. Order hepatic transaminases, direct Coomb's test (r/o immune-mediated hemolysis), fractionated bilirubin, CBC, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin (decreased in hemolysis), and a urinalysis for urobilinogen or hemoglobinuria.
To confirm G6PD deficiency, order a test of G6PD enzyme activity—a fluorescent antibody test for hemoglobin-adjusted NADPH or a PCR genotype test.

Several RDTs are available. Field testing in Haiti of CareStartTM G6PD test, a qualitative visual dye colorization test, found a negative predictive value of 98.2%, making this an excellent test for determining which patients are able to take primaquine safely. CareStart was 90% sensitive for detecting individuals with severe deficiency and 84.8% sensitive for detecting individuals with moderate and severe deficiency vs. the quantitative Trinity Biotech assay.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of data from 8 studies with 5,777 results found CareStartTM G6PD had a pooled sensitivity of 96% (95% CI 90-99) and a specificity of 95% (95% CI 92-96) at a threshold of enzyme activity <30% normal. Varying the prevalence of G6PDd from 5% to 30%, the unconditional negative predictive value was 0.99 (95% CI 0.94-1.00), with a positive likelihood ratio of 18.23 (95% CI 13.04-25.48) and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.05 (95% CI 0.02-0.12). Test performance was significantly better in males

Field testing of BinaxNOW, a qualitative enzyme chromatographic test for G6PD enzyme activity detection, in subjects in Brazil, Peru, Thailand, and India found similar high specificity (100%) with lower sensitivity (54.5%)..

Another RDT (60 minutes) using an automated UV-based enzymatic assay (Mindray, PRC) compared to a spectrophotometric assay in 251 blood samples had a sensitivity of 85.7%, specificity of 99.2%, and positive and negative predictive values 85.7% and 99.2%, respectively. The assay was limited for identifying individuals with intermediate G6PD enzyme activity.

A point-of-care quantitative test, STANDARD™ G6PD test (SD Biosensor, Suwon, South Korea), performed equivalently to a reference assay for diagnosing G6PD deficiency (< 30% normal) with a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI 95.7-100) and specificity of 97% (95% CI: 94.5-98.5). This test was able to identify females with <70% normal G6PD activity with a sensitivity of 95.5% and specificity of 97%.

In a Chinese population study, use of a rapid, batch-based detection test called “Amplification Refractory Mutation System combined with Melting Curve Analysis (ARMS-MC)," enabled detection of the 6 most common G6PD mutations that was consistent with results of direct sequencing with 100% accuracy and specificity.
In neonates, order ABO and Rh tests to determine if hemolysis is due to blood group or Rh incompatibility.

Suspect G6PD deficiency in neonates with jaundice and with older patients who present with hemolytic anemia, particularly if there is possible triggering by a medication (), food, or stressor such as infection or diabetic ketoacidosis.
Order hepatic transaminases and Coomb's test. If transaminases are abnormal, suspect hepatitis. If normal transaminases and Coomb's test is negative, suspect G6PD deficiency.
To confirm G6PD deficiency, order a test of G6PD enzyme activity—a fluorescent antibody test for hemoglobin-adjusted NADPH or a PCR genotype test.
Remove the offending drug () or food substance. C
Provide supportive care and consider blood transfusion for severe anemia. C
Consider clofibrate therapy in severe G6PD-deficiency-related neonatal jaundice. A
Consider splenectomy for severe cases.
Treatment for hemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency is primarily supportive, with oxygen, adequate fluids, and bed rest.
Clofibrate more rapidly reduces severity of G6PD-related jaundice in neonatates.

After the destruction of older erythrocytes that have decreased G6PD activity, younger erythrocytes and reticulocytes have enough G6PD to withstand further oxidative stress. In most cases, removal of the inciting substance or drug is sufficient to prevent serious complications.
Dialysis may be needed in cases of acute renal failure.
Avoid food and medication indicated in .
In the future, it may be possible via gene therapy to selectively enhance transcription of G6PD using HDAC inhibitors.
Consider referral or hospitalization for patients with hemoglobinuria, severe jaundice, splenomegaly, or symptoms of acute chest syndrome.
Prognosis is usually very good, with occasional periods of exacerbation due to exposure to oxidative substances or physiological conditions. C
May cause neonatal jaundice, typically within 4 days of birth.

In an Israeli population study of 2656 newborns (of 3770 born) who were screened as part of a universal newborn screening program, 2.7% were G6PD-deficient (G6PD <2.0 U/g Hb) and 1.8% had borderline G6PD activity (2-7 U/g Hb). The highest prevalence was for children of Sephardic Jewish or Muslim Arab heritage (10.7% and 6.2%, respectively). Significantly more children with G6PD deficiency or borderline activity required phototherapy compared to children with normal G6PD.

In two American population studies of white infants of 35 or more weeks gestation, mean G6PD activity levels were 12.3 ± 3.1 U/g Hb and 13.3 ± 1.8 U/g Hb in the retrospective and prospective studies, respectively. This level was higher than seen in white adults. The authors suggested use of activity levels less than 7 u/g Hb as indicative of G6PD deficiency.
Neonates may at times require exchange transfusions for severe hyperbilirubinemia to avoid kernicterus.
G6PD deficiency was seen in 21% of kernicterus cases in 1 registry study.

In a Canadian study, of 91 cases of severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, of the 57 cases (63%) for which a cause was identified, ABO incompatibility was the cause in 35 patients and G6PD deficiency in 11 patients.

Short-term administration of analgesics may be safe; in one study of 10 children with G6PD deficiency, 3 days of postoperative administration of analgesics including paracetamol, ibuprofen, or tramadol did not cause hemolysis.
